    JavaScript Statement

  • JavaScript statements are composed of:
    • Values
    • Operators
    • Expressions
    • Keywords
    • Comments
  • Below is an example of a statement:
    •                     
    var x, y, z;    // Statement 1
x = 5;          // Statement 2
y = 6;          // Statement 3
z = x + y;      // Statement 4
document.getElementById("demod").innerHTML = "Hasil dari " + x + " + " + y + " adalah " + z; // Statement 5
  • Statements above will be rendered as:

  • What that code does is it will calculate the value of x + y and then display the result in the element with id="demod"
  • JavaScript statements will be executed one by one in the same order as it's written
  • Statements are separated by semicolons (;)
  • White spaces and line breaks are ignored in JavaScript, but the best practice is to use them around operators to make the code more readable
  • It is also advised to make a line of JavaScript code, not longer than 80 characters.
  • If a statement is too long, it can be split into a new lines. The best place to break a statement is after an operator like below:
    •                     
    document.getElementById("demod").innerHTML =
"Hasil dari " + x + " + " + y + " adalah " + z;
  • Multiple statements can be grouped together using curly brackets ({})
  • This usually used in functions, loops, and conditional statements
  • Below is an example of how to use curly brackets:
    •                     
    function myFunction() {
    document.getElementById("demoe").innerHTML = "Hi there";
    document.getElementById("demof").innerHTML = "How are you?";
}
  • Code above will be rendered as:

  • There are a list of reserved words in JavaScript that cannot be used as variable names, function names, or any other identifiers. Which can be seen here

JavaScript Syntax

  • Syntax is the set of rules of how a programs are constructed

    • JavaScript Values

  • The JavaScript syntax defines two types of values:
    • Fixed values
    • Variable values
  • Fixed values are called literals. Variable values are called variables
  • The two most important syntax for literals or fixed values are:
    • Numbers can be written with or without decimals:

      99

      92.42

    • Strings are text, written within double or single quotes:

      "Hello World!"

      'Hello World!'

  • Next is JavaScript variables
  • In programming, variables are used to store data values
  • An equal sign is used to assign values to variables
  • JavaScript uses the var, let, and const keywords to declare variables, or declared automatically like this:

    • a = 9; //declared automatically

    let b = 5;

    var c = 6;

    const d = 7;

    (a + b + c) * d;

  • Below is the difference of those three:
    • Keyword Scope Can be redeclared Can be reassigned
    var Function Yes Yes
    let Block No Yes
    const Block No No
    Declared automatically Global Yes Yes

    >When to Use var, let, or const?

    1. Always declare variables

    2. Always use const if the value should not be changed

    3. Always use const if the type should not be changed (Arrays and Objects)

    4. Only use let if you can't use const

    5. Only use var if you MUST support old browsers.

  • It is not recomended to declare a variable automatically, as it will be accessible globally and can lead to unexpected behavior like this:

    • let output = '';

    function testImplicitGlobal() {

        if (true) {

            xx = 10; // `xx` is implicitly declared as a global variable

            output += "Inside if block: " + xx; // This will log 10

        }

        output += "Outside if block: " + xx; // This will also log 10 because `xx` is a global variable

    }

    testImplicitGlobal();

    // Demonstrate potential conflict with another function

    function anotherFunction() {

        xx = 20; // This modifies the same global variable `xx`

    }

    anotherFunction();

    output += "After calling anotherFunction, xx is: " + xx; // This will log 20

    return output;

  • Notes: The let and const are block-scoped, while the var is function-scoped
  • Block-scoped means that the variable is only available within the block of code where it's declared, like this:

    • let output = '';

    if (true) {

        let y = 20; // `y` is block-scoped to this `if` block

        output += "Inside if block: " + y; // This will log 20

    }

    output += "Outside if block: " + (typeof y); // This will log 'undefined' because `y` is not accessible outside the block

    return output;

  • Function-scoped means that the variable is available within the function where it's declared, like this:

    • let output = '';

    function testFunctionScope() {

        if (true) {

            var x = 10; // `x` is function-scoped to `testFunctionScope`

            output += "Inside if block: " + x; // This will log 10

        }

        output += "Outside if block: " + x; // This will also log 10 because `x` is accessible throughout the function

    }

    testFunctionScope();

    return output;

  • It is also possible to declare a variable and assign a value later like this:

    • var a;

    a = 8;

    JavaScript Operators

  • JavaScript uses arithmetic operators to compute values (+ - * /) to compute values

    • (5 + 10) * 2 - (12 / 3)

  • An expression is a combination of values, variables, and operators, which computes to a value.
  • The computation is called an evaluation.
  • For example, 5 * 10 evaluates to 50:

    • 5 * 10

  • The value itself can be of various types, such as numbers, strings, or objects like this:

    • 5 + 10 + " " + "Hello" + " " + "World"

  • To comment in JavaScript, use // for single line comment, and /* */ for multi-line comment like this:

    • /* This is a

    multi-line comment */

    // This is a single line comment

    JavaScript identifiers / Names

  • In JavaScript, names are called identifiers. It is used to name variables, functions, classes, and objects
  • The rules for legal identifiers are much the same in most programming languages:
    • The first character must be a letter (A - Z or a - z), an underscore (_), or a dollar sign ($)
    • Subsequent characters may be letters, digits, underscores, or dollar signs
    • Numbers are not allowed as the first character
    • JavaScript is case-sensitive. so variable lastname and lastName are two different variables
    • Reserved words (like JavaScript keywords) cannot be used as identifiers
  • There are various ways to name variable with multiple words like this:
    • using_underscore
    • UpperCamelCase
    • lowerCamelCase (this is the one that mostly used in Javascript program)

    *Notes: Even tho the other two are valid, the lowerCamelCase is the most used in JavaScript. In the other hand, it is not allowed to use hyphen (-) in variable name

    Assignment Operators

  • In JavaScript, the equal sign (=) is an assignment operator, not an equality operator
  • Below is the example:

    • x = 10; // Assign the value 10 to x

    y = 10; // Assign the value 10 to y

    x == y; // Returns true because the values are equal

    Data Types

  • JavaScript variables can hold many data types: numbers, strings, objects, arrays, functions, and more
  • Strings are written either with single or double quotes, numbers are written without quotes

    • let x = 5, // Number

    y = 'John', // String

    z = true, // Boolean

    a = null, // Null

    b, // Undefined

    c = [1, 2, 3], // Array

    d = {firstName: 'John', lastName: 'Doe'}; // Object

JavaScript Operators

  • There are various types of operators in JavaScript:
    • Arithmetic Operators
    • Assignment Operators
    • Comparison Operators
    • String Operators
    • Logical Operators
    • Bitwise Operators
    • Ternary Operators
    • Type Operators

    JavaScript Arithmetic Operators

  • JavaScript arithmetic operators are used to perform arithmetic on numbers
  • Below is the list of arithmetic operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    + Addition 10 + 5 = 15
    - Subtraction 10 - 5 = 5
    * Multiplication 10 * 5 = 50
    ** Exponentiation 10 ** 5 = 100000
    / Division 10 / 5 = 2
    % Modulus (division remainder) 10 % 5 = 0
    ++ Increment 10++ = 11
    -- Decrement 10-- = 9
  • Arithmetic operators can be used on a literals, variables, or expressions like this:

    • let output = '';

    function arithmeticOperations() {

        let a = 10;

        let b = 20;

        let x = 100 + 50;

        output += "Literal Number Addition: 100 + 50 = " + x + " | ";

        let y = x + a + b;

        output += "Variable Addition: x + a + b = " + y + " | ";

        let z = (y ** 2 + b) % (a * 2);

        output += "Expression: (y ** 2 + b) % (a * 2) = " + z;

    }

    arithmeticOperations();

    return output;

  • Javascript generally has the same rule as daily math; the operator with the highest precedence will be executed first like this:

    • 5 + 10 * 2

  • The complete precedence will be explained in later section

    • JavaScript Assignment Operators

  • Assignment operators are used to assign values to variables
  • Below is the list of assignment operators:
    • Operator Example Same As Explanation
    = x = y x = y Assigns the value of y to x
    += x += y x = x + y Adds y to x
    -= x -= y x = x - y Subtracts y from x
    *= x *= y x = x * y Multiplies x by y
    /= x /= y x = x / y Divides x by y
    %= x %= y x = x % y Assigns the remainder of x divided by y to x
    **= x **= y x = x ** y Assigns the result of x to the power of y to x

    Operator Example Same As Explanation
    <<= x <<= y x = x << y Shifts x in binary representation y bits to the left, shifting in zeros from the right
    >>= x >>= y x = x >> y Shifts x in binary representation y bits to the right, discarding bits shifted off
    >>>= x >>>= y x = x >>> y Shifts x in binary representation y bits to the right, discarding bits shifted off, and shifting in zeros from the left

    Operator Example Same As Explanation
    &= x &= y x = x & y Assign the result of bitwise AND of x and y to x
    |= x |= y x = x | y Assign the result of bitwise OR of x and y to x
    ^= x ^= y x = x ^ y Assign the result of bitwise XOR of x and y to x

    Operator Example Same As Explanation
    &&= x &&= y x = x && (x = y) Assign the result of logical AND of x and y to x
    ||= x ||= y x = x || (x = y) Assign the result of logical OR of x and y to x
    ??= x ??= y x = x ?? (x = y) Assigns a y to x if x is null or undefined

    JavaScript Comparison Operators

  • Comparison operators are used in logical statements to determine equality or difference between variables or values
  • Below is the list of comparison operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    == Equal to x == y
    === Equal value and equal type x === y
    != Not equal x != y
    !== Not equal value or not equal type x !== y
    > Greater than x > y
    < Less than x < y
    >= Greater than or equal to x >= y
    <= Less than or equal to x <= y
    ? Ternary operator x = y ? a : b
  • It is possible to do String comparison and addition like this:

    • let output = '';

    function stringCompareAddition() {

        let x = 'Iqbal ';

        let y = 'Dzakwan |';

        output += "String addition: " + x + y;

        output += " String comparison: " + (x != y);

    }

    stringCompareAddition();

    return output;

  • When used on a string, the + operator is called concatenation operator
  • Adding string with a number will have a result of string like this:

    • 'Iqbal ' + 2024

    JavaScript Logical Operators

  • Logical operators are used to determine the logic between variables or values
  • Below is the list of logical operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    && Logical and x && y
    || Logical or x || y
    ! Logical not !x
  • Below is the example of how to use those operators:

    • let output = '';

    function logicalOperators() {

        let x = 10;

        let y = 5;

        output += "Logical AND: " + (x && y);

        output += " Logical OR: " + (x || y);

        output += " Logical NOT: " + (!x);

    }

    logicalOperators();

    return output;

  • Notes: It will be explained more in later section

    • JavaScript Bitwise Operators

  • Bit operators work on 32 bits numbers.
  • Any numeric operand in the operation is converted into a 32 bit number.
  • Below is the list of bitwise operators:
    • Operator Description Example Same as Result Decimal
    & AND 5 & 1 0101 & 0001 0001 1
    | OR 5 | 1 0101 | 0001 0101 5
    ~ NOT ~ 5 ~0101 1010 10
    ^ XOR 5 ^ 1 0101 ^ 0001 0100 4
    << Left shift 5 << 1 0101 << 1 1010 10
    >> Right shift 5 >> 1 0101 >> 1 0010 2
    >>> Unsigned right shift 5 >>> 1 0101 >>> 1 0010 2

    The examples above uses 4 bits unsigned examples. But JavaScript uses 32-bit signed numbers.

    Because of this, in JavaScript, ~ 5 will not return 10. It will return -6.

    ~00000000000000000000000000000101 will return 11111111111111111111111111111010

    JavaScript Ternary Operators

  • Ternary operators are used to assign a value to a variable based on some condition
  • Below is the example of how to use ternary operators:

    • let output = '';

    function ternaryOperators() {

        let x = 10;

        output += "x is " + (x > 10 ? 'Greater than 10' : 'Less than 10');

    }

    ternaryOperators();

    return output;

    Javascript Type Operators

  • Type operators are used to determine the type of a variable or value
  • Below is the list of type operators:
    • Operator Description Example
    typeof Returns the type of a variable typeof x
    instanceof Returns true if an object is an instance of an object type object instanceof type
  • Below is the example of how to use those operators:

    • let output = '';

    function typeOperators() {

        let x = 10;

        output += "Type of x: " + (typeof x) + " | ";

        let y = {name: 'Iqbal', age: 23, city: 'Morowali'};

        output += "Instance of y: " + (y instanceof Object);

    }

    typeOperators();

    return output;

  • Notes: It will be explained more in later section

JavaScript Data Types

  • Javascript has 8 Data Types:
    • String
  • String is a series of characters like 'Iqbal Dzakwan'

    • //Using single quotes:

    let x = 'Iqbal Dzakwan';

    //Using double quotes:

    let y = "Iqbal Dzakwan";

  • It is possible to use quotes inside a string, as long as they don't match the quotes surrounding the string:

    • //Using single quote inside double quotes:

    let x = "Iqbal's";

    //Using double quotes inside single quotes:

    let y = 'Iqbal "Dzakwan"';

    Number
  • Number are stored as 64-bit floating point numbers. It can be written with or without decimals like 10 or 10.00

    • // Without decimals:

    let x = 10;

    // With decimals:

    let y = 10.00;

  • It is possible to use scientific notation for extra small or extra large number like this:

    • let x = 123e5; // 12300000

    let y = 123e-5; // 0.00123

    Most programming languages have many number types:


    Whole numbers (integers):

    byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit)


    Real numbers (floating-point):

    float (32-bit), double (64-bit).


    Javascript numbers are always one type:

    double (64-bit floating point).

    BigInt
  • JavaScript BigInt is a new datatype (ES2020) that can be used to store integer values that are too big to be represented by a normal JavaScript Number.

    • let x = BigInt(1234567890123456789012345678901234567890);

    Boolean
  • Boolean can only have two values: true or false

    • let output = '';

    function booleanOperations() {

        let x = 5;

        let y = 5;

        let z = 6;

        output += "x == y: " + (x == y) + " | ";

        output += "x == z: " + (x == z) + " | ";

    }

    booleanOperations();

    return output;

    Array
  • Array is a special variable, which can hold more than one value at a time. array indexes are zero based, which means the first item is [0], second is [1], and so on.

    • let cars = ['Toyota', 'Honda', 'Suzuki'];

    Object
  • Object is a special variable, which can hold many values. It is written as name:value pairs, separated by commas, inside curly braces {}.

    • let person = {name: 'Iqbal', age: 23, city: 'Morowali'};

  • The object (person) in the example above has 3 properties: name, age, and city.
    • Undefined
  • Undefined means a variable has been declared but has not been assigned a value.

    • let x;

  • It is also possible to empty an already defined variable so that it's value will be undefined, as well as it's type

    • let output = '';

    function undefinedVariable() {

        let x = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];

        output += "original x: " + x + " | ";

        output += "type of x: " + typeof x + " | ";

        x = undefined;

        output += "x now: " + x + " | ";

        output += "type of x now: " + typeof x + " | ";

    }

    undefinedVariable();

    return output;

    Empty Value
  • An empty value has nothing to do with undefined.
  • String with an empty value, will have a value of "" and its type still string. While in undefined, it doesn't have a value and its type is undefined.

    • let car = ""; // The value is "", the typeof is "string"

JavaScript Functions

  • A JavaScript function is a block of code designed to perform a particular task.
  • A JavaScript function is executed when "something" invokes it (calls it).
  • Below is the syntax of a function:

    • function name(parameter1, parameter2, parameter3) {

        // code to be executed

    }

  • JavaScript function is defined with the function keyword, followed by a name, followed by parentheses ().
  • Function names can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs (same rules as variables)
  • The parentheses may include parameter names separated by commas
  • The code to be executed, by the function, is placed inside curly brackets: {}
  • Function parameters are the names listed inside the parentheses () in the function definition.
  • Function arguments are the values received by the function when it is invoked.
  • Inside the function, the arguments (the parameters) behave as local variables.

    • Function Invocation

  • The code inside the function will execute when "something" invokes (calls) the function:
    • When an event occurs (like when a user clicks a button)
    • When it is invoked (called) from JavaScript code
    • Automatically (self invoked)

    Function Return

  • When JavaScript reaches a return statement, the function will stop executing.
  • If the function was invoked from a statement, JavaScript will "return" to execute the code after the invoking statement.
  • Functions often compute a return value. The return value is "returned" back to the "caller":

    • // Function is called, return value will end up in x

    let x = myFunction(4, 3);

    function myFunction(a, b) {

        return a + b;

    }

    So, why using functions?

    Functions are used to perform certain actions, and they are important for code reusability.

    For example, you can use the same code many times with different arguments, to produce different results.

    The () Operator

  • The () operator invokes (calls) the function:

    • let output = '';

    function toCelsius(fahrenheit) {

        return (5/9) * (fahrenheit-32);

    output += toCelsius();

    }

    return output;

  • Accessing a function with incorrect parameters can return an incorrect answer:

    • function toCelsius(f) {

        return (5/9) * (f-32);

    }

    let value = toCelsius();

    return value;

  • Accessing a function without () returns the function and not the function result:

    • function toCelsius(fahrenheit) {

        return (5/9) * (fahrenheit-32);

    }

    let value = toCelsius;

    return value;

    Function Naming

    Function names can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs (same rules as variables)

    The parentheses may include parameter names separated by commas

    The code to be executed, by the function, is placed inside curly brackets: {}

    Function parameters are the names listed inside the parentheses () in the function definition.

    Function arguments are the values received by the function when it is invoked.

    Inside the function, the arguments (the parameters) behave as local variables.

    Function as Variable Values

  • Functions can be used the same way as how variables are used. It can be assigned to a variable, and the variable can be used to call the function:

    • Instead of using a variable to store the return value of a function like this:

    let x = toCelsius(77);

    let text = "The temperature is " + x + " Celsius";

    You can use the function directly like this:

    let text = "The temperature is " + toCelsius(77) + "°" + " Celsius";

    Local Variables

  • Variables declared within a JavaScript function, become local to the function.
  • Local variables can only be accessed from within the function, and will be deleted when the function is completed.
  • This mean, the same variable name can be used in different functions

    • // code here can NOT use carName


    function myFunction() {

        let carName = "Volvo";

        // code here CAN use carName

    }


    // code here can NOT use carName

JavaScript Objects

  • Object is a special variable, which can hold many values. It is written as name:value pairs, separated by commas, inside curly braces {}.

    • const car = {type: 'Fiat', model: '500', color: 'white'};

  • Object can also has methods like car.start, car.drive, car.stop, etc.
  • Methods are performed at different times

    • Note:

    It is a common practice to declare objects with the const keyword. This tells the browser that the object will not be reassigned, and it will be faster to access the object.

    JavaScript object can be defined through object literal, using the new keyword, or using an object constructor

    Javascript Object Literal

  • An object literal is a list of name:value pairs (like type:Fiat) inside curly braces {} and are separated by commas.

    • {type: 'Fiat', model: '500', color: 'white'};

  • These examples create a JavaScript object wirh 4 properties:

    • const person = {firstName: 'John', lastName: 'Doe', age: 50, eyeColor: 'blue'};

    It is also possible to create it like this:

    const person = {

        firstName: 'John',

        lastName: 'Doe',

        age: 50,

        eyeColor: 'blue'

    };

    An object can also created as an empty object, and then add the properties later:

    // Create an empty Object

    const person = {};


    // Add properties to the object

    person.firstName = 'John';

    person.lastName = 'Doe';

    person.age = 50;

    person.eyeColor = 'blue';

    Using <new >Keyword

  • Below is the example on how to create a new JavaScript object using the new keyword, and then adds 4 properties:

    • // Create an Object

    const person = new Object();


    // Add properties to the object

    person.firstName = 'John';

    person.lastName = 'Doe';

    person.age = 50;

    person.eyeColor = 'blue';

    Note:

    Both examples above do exactly the same, and it is recomended to just use the Object Literal for a better readability, simplicity, and performance.

    Using Object Constructor

  • Below is the example on how to create a new JavaScript object using an object constructor, and then adds 4 properties:

    • // Create an Object Constructor

    function Person(firstName, lastName, age, eyeColor) {

        this.firstName = firstName;

        this.lastName = lastName;

        this.age = age;

        this.eyeColor = eyeColor;

    }

    After declaring the constructor, now we can use new Person() to create many new Person objects:

    const myFather = new Person('John', 'Doe', 50, 'blue');

    const myMother = new Person('Sally', 'Rally', 48, 'green');

    const myBrother = new Person('Bob', 'Doe', 25, 'brown');

  • *Notes:
    • It is considered good practice to name constructor functions with an upper-case first letter
    • In the constructor function, this has no value. The value of this will become the new object when a new object is created
    Property Default Values
  • A value given to a property will be a default value for all objects created by the constructor:

    • this.nationality = 'Indonesian';

    return myFather.nationality;

    Adding Property to a Constructor
  • To add a new property into the constructor, must use construction function prototype like this:

    • //Adding new property

    Person.prototype.nationality = 'Indonesian';


    //Adding new method

    Person.prototype.name = function() {

        return this.firstName + ' ' + this.lastName;

    }

    Built-in JavaScript Constructors
  • JavaScript has several built-in constructors for all native JavaScript objects:

    • new Object() //A new Object object

    new Array() //A new Array object

    new Map() //A new Map object

    new Set() //A new Set object

    new Date() //A new Date object

    new RegExp() //A new RegExp object

    new Function() //A new Function object

    Note:

    The Math() object is not in the list. Math is a global object. The new keyword cannot be used to create a new Math object.

  • There are alternatives on how to create a new object instead of using the new keyword:

    • let a = {} //Object object

    let b = [] //Array object

    let c = /()/ //Regexp object

    let d = function(){} //Function object

    Object Properties

    Property Value
    firstName John
    lastName Doe
    age 50
    eyeColor blue
  • Object properties can be accessed in three ways:

    • // objectName.propertyName

    let age = person.age;


    // objectName["propertyName"]

    let age = person['age'];


    // objectName[expression]

    let x = 'age';

  • Below is the example on how to access the object properties:

    • objectName.propertyName


    function person(fname, lname) {

        this.firstname = fname;

        this.lastname = lname;

    }

    const myFather = new person('John', 'Doe');

    const myMother = new person('Sally', 'Rally');

    return 'My father is ' + myFather.firstname + ' ' + myFather.lastname '. My mother is ' + myMother.firstname + ' ' + myMother.lastname;


    objectName["propertyName"]


    function person(fname, lname) {

        this.firstname = fname;

        this.lastname = lname;

    }

    const myFather = new person('John', 'Doe');

    const myMother = new person('Sally', 'Rally');

    return 'My father is ' + myFather['firstname'] + ' ' + myFather['lastname'] '. My mother is ' + myMother['firstname'] + ' ' + myMother['lastname'];


    objectName[expression]


    function car(brand, type, price, disc) {

        this.brand = brand;

        this.type = type;

        this.price = price;

        this.disc = disc;

        this.dcprice = function() {

            return this.price - (this.price * this.disc);

        }

    const supra = new car('Toyota', 'Supra', 100000, 0.12);

    let x = 'brand';

    let y = 'type';

    let z = 'dcprice';

    return supra[x] + ' ' + supra[y] + ' price after discount is $' + supra[z]() + '.';


  • Below is how to add and delete an Object Properties.
    • Adding New Properties

    supra.topSpeed = 310;

    return supra.brand + ' ' + supra.type ' has the top speed of ' + supra.topSpeed 'km/h.';

    Deleting Properties

    //deleting discount percentage

    delete supra.disc;

    return supra[x] + ' ' + supra[y] + ' price after discount is $' + supra[z]() + '.';

    Nested Objects
  • Property values inside an object can actually be other objects:

    • const car = {

        brand: 'Toyota',

        type: 'Supra',

        price: 100000,

        disc: 0.12,

        dcprice: function() {

            return this.price - (this.price * this.disc);

        },

        topSpeed: 310,

        model: {

            supra1: 'Celica XX',

            supra2: 'Celica Supra',

            supra3: 'A70 Supra',

            supra4: 'A80 Supra',

            supra5: 'GR Supra',

        }

    };

  • To access the nested object, you can use dot notation or bracket notation just like accessing objects as usual like this:

    • supra.brand + ' ' + supra.type ' has a long history. The first generation is the ' + supra.model.supra1 + '.' +
    ' The second generation, '     + supra.model['supra2'] ', is the last version that has the name 'Celica'.
    The latest one launched after years of hiatus from the market at 2019 as '     + supra['model']['supra5'] .'

    Object Methods

  • Methods are actions that can be performed on objects
  • Methods are function definitions stored as property values
    • Property Property Value
    firstName John
    lastName Doe
    age 50
    eyeColor blue
    fullName function() {return this.firstName + " " + this.lastName;}
  • Methods are accessed like this:

    • objectName.methodName()

  • Below is the example on how to access the object methods:

    • function person(fname, lname, id) { //method fullname doesnt need to be declared as a variable

        this.fname = fname;

        this.lname = lname;

        this.id = id;

        this.fullname = function() {

            return this.fname + ' ' + this.lname;

        }

    const employee = new person('Andy', 'Roe', 9969);

    return employee.fullname() + ' with ID number ' + employee.id + ' is the Employee of The year of 2023';

    Objects are containers for Properties and Methods

    Properties are named values

    Methods are functions stored as properties

    Properties can be primities values, functions, or even other objects

    All Javascript values exept primitives are objects

    JavaScript Primitives

  • A Primitive value is a value that has no properties or methods
  • There are 8 primitive data types in JavaScript:
    • string
    • number
    • bigint
    • boolean
    • null
    • undefined
    • bigint
    • symbol

    Immutable:

    Primitives are immutable (they are hardcoded and therefore cannot be changed)

    Even if you assign a new value to a string, the old value will still be there

    Displaying JavaScript Object

  • There are several ways to display JavaScript objects:
    • Displaying the Object Properties by name
    • Displaying the Object Properties in a Loop
    • Displaying the Object using Object.values()
    • Displaying the Object using JSON.stringify()
    Displaying the Object Properties by name

    const civic = new car('Honda', 'Civic', 1427500000, 0.05);

    civic.model = 'Type R';

    let formattedPrice = civic.dcprice().toLocaleString('id-ID');

    return 'Unleash the thrill of the drive with the ' + civic.brand + ' ' + civic.type + ' ' + civic.model +
    ', where performance meets precision in every mile, starting at Rp ' + formattedPrice;

    Displaying the Object Properties in a Loop

    const supra = new car('Toyota', 'Supra', 2237600000, 0.05);

    const civic = new car('Honda', 'Civic', 1427500000, 0.05);

    const brz = new car('Subaru', 'BRZ', 845000000, 0.05);

    const m3 = new car('BMW', 'M3', 2612114000, 0.05);

    const mustang = new car('Ford', 'Mustang GT', 2400000000, 0.05);


    const cars = [supra, civic, brz, m3, mustang];

    let text = '';

    for let i in cars; i;) {

        const downPayment = cars[i].dp().toLocaleString('id-ID');

        const monthlyPayment = cars[i].installment().toLocaleString('id-ID');

        text += '<li>

                     <span style="color: black; font-weight: bold;">${cars[i].brand} ${cars[i].type}</span> -

                     <del style="color: #afafaf;">Price: Rp ${cars[i].price.toLocaleString('id-ID')}</del> -

                     <span style="color: black; font-weight: bold;">Down Payment: Rp ${downPayment}</span><br>

                     <span style="color: black; font-weight: bold;">Monthly Installments: Only Rp ${monthlyPayment} over a 5-year term

                 </li>'

    }

    return "<h5 style='margin-top:0; margin-bottom:4px;'>Explore Our Premium Car Collection:</h5><ul>" + text + "</ul>";

    Using Object.values()
  • Object.values() creates an array from the property values:

    • //create an object

    const car = {

        brand: 'Toyota',

        year: 2023,

        type: 'Yaris'

    };


    //create an array

    const myCAr = Object.values(car);


    //display the array

    return myCAr;

    Using Object.entries()
  • Object.entries() makes it simple to use objects in loops:

    • const fruits = {bananas:300, oranges:200, apples:430};


    let text = "";

    for(let [fruit, value] of Object.entries(fruits)){

        text += fruit + ": " + value + "<br>";

    }

    return text;

    Using JSON.stringify()
  • JavaScript objects can be converted to a string with JSON method JSON.stringify()
  • The result will be a string written in JSON format

    • let myString = JSON.stringify(car);

    JavaScript Immutable Primitive

  • Immutable mean that the value of a variable cannot be changed directly after it has been created. If you want to change the value of a primitive, you have to assign a new value to the variable, but the old value will still be there.

    • let x = 10; // x holds 10

    let y = x; // y also holds 10 (value 10 is not modified, just referenced)

    x = 45; // x now holds 45, but y still holds 10

    console(x); // Output: 45

    console(y); // Output: 10 (y still references the original value 10)

  • This would be different for mutable objects like arrays and objects

    • let x = {name: 'John', age: 25}; // x holds an object

    let y = x; // y also holds the same object

    x.name = 'Jane'; // x.name is now 'Jane'

    console(x); // Output: {name: 'Jane', age: 25} (x changes its value)

    console(y); // Output: {name: 'Jane', age: 25} (y references the new value of x)

    JavaScript Mutable Objects

  • Mutable means that the value of a variable can be changed directly after it has been created. If you want to change the value of an object, you can do so by changing the value of the object directly like this:

    • //Create an Object Constructor

    function person(fname, lname, age) {

        this.fname = fname;

        this.lname = lname;

        this.age = age;

        this.fulldata = function() {

            return this.fname + ' ' + this.lname + ', age: ' + this.age;

    }


    //Create object employee based on person constructor

    const employee = new person('Parjo', 'Kui', 36);


    //Create a copy of object employee

    const x = employee;


    //Change the value of the copy, which will also change the value of original employee object

    x.age = 32;

    return employee.fulldata() + ' is the prime suspect of this case.';

JavaScript Events

  • An HTML event can be something the browser does, or something a user does.
  • Here are some examples of HTML events:
    • When a user clicks the mouse
    • When a web page has loaded
    • When an image has been loaded
    • When the mouse moves over an element
    • When an input field is changed
    • When an HTML form is submitted
    • When a user strokes a key
  • JavaScript lets you execute code when events are detected
  • HTML allows event handler attributes, with JavaScript code, to be added to HTML elements
  • In the following example, an onclick attribute (with code), is added to a <button> element:

    • <button onclick="document.getElementById('demo').innerHTML = Date()">The time is?</button>

    <p id="demo"></p>

  • It is also possible to make something like this using this.innerHTML that would change the content of its own element
  • It is more common to see event attributes calling a JavaScript function like this:

    • function displayDate() {

        document('#demoa16').innerHTML = Date();

    }


    <button onclick="displayDate()">The time is?</button>

  • Here is a list of some common HTML events:
    • onchange - An HTML element has been changed
    • onclick - The user clicks an HTML element
    • onmouseover - The user moves the mouse over an HTML element
    • onmouseout - The user moves the mouse away from an HTML element
    • onkeydown - The user pushes a keyboard key
    • onkeyup - The user releases a keyboard key
    • onload - The browser has finished loading the page
  • For a complete list of events, visit HTML Event Attributes

JavaScript Strings

  • Strings are used for storing text
  • Strings are written with quotes
  • JavaScript string is zero or more characters written inside single or double quotes:

    • let carName = 'Volvo'; // Using single quotes

    let carModel = "XC90"; // Using double quotes

  • Its possible to use quotes inside a string, as long they don't match the quotes surrounding the string:

    • let txt = "It's alright";

    let txt = 'He said "Hello"';

  • If you want to use the same type of quotes inside a string, you have to escape them in JavaScript, or use HTML Entities for HTML:

    • //Using escape character

    let txt = "We are the so-called \"Vikings\" from the north.";


    //Using HTML Entities for HTML

    <p>He said &quot;Hello&quot;</p>

    Template Strings
  • Templates are strings enclosed in backticks (`this is a template string`)
  • Templates allow single and double quotes inside a string

    • let txt = `It's alright. That's just a "small" mistakes`;

    Interpolation
  • Template strings can be used for string interpolation
  • Interpolation is the process of evaluating a string literal containing one or more placeholders, yielding a result in which the placeholders are replaced with their corresponding values
    • Syntax:

    ${...}

    Variable Substitution
  • Template strings can be used to substitute variables:

    • let brand = 'Toyota';

    let type = 'Supra';

    let car = `No problem, here is information about ${brand} ${type}.`;

    return car;

    Expression Substitution
  • Template strings can be used to substitute expressions:

    • let price = 2237600000;

    let dpCicil = `With Down Payment of Rp ${(0.2 * price).toLocaleString('id-ID')} and payment only at
    Rp ${(((0.8 * price) * 0.02 * (1 + 0.02) ** 180) / ((1 + 0.02) ** 180 - 1)).toLocaleString('id-ID')}
    per month for 15 years`    ;

    return dpCicil;

    HTML Templates
  • Template strings can be used to create HTML templates:

    • let header = 'Template Strings';

    let tags = ['template strings', 'javascript', 'es6'];

    let html = `<h2 style="margin: 0;">${header}</h2><ul>`;


    for (const x of tags) {

        html += `<li>${x}</li>`;

    }

    html += `</ul>`;

    return html;

    Breaking Long Lines
  • For readability, programmers often like to avoid long code lines. A safe way to break up a statement is after an operator.
  • A safe way to break up a string is by using string addition:

    • let txt = 'We are the so-called "Vikings" from the north.' +

    'We are the so-called "Vikings" from the north.';

    String Methods

  • JavaScript strings are primitive and immutable; this mean that all string methods will return a new string, not modify the original string
  • Here are the lists of JavaScript String methods:
    at()
  • The at() method returns the character at a specified index (position) in a string. It support negative index, and will access the string from the end of the string. Calling at() with an index outside of the string will return undefined
    • Syntax:

    string.at(index)


    let text = "The light from the streetlamp was bright and eerie.";

    let at1 = text.at(1);

    let at2 = text.at(2);

    let at3 = text.at(5);

    let at4 = text.at(4);

    let at5 = text..at(3);

    let at6 = text.at(1);

    let at7 = text.at(2);

    let at8 = text.at(-10);

    let at9 = text.at(8);

    let at10 = text.at(2);

    let at11 = text.at(-4);

    let at11 = text.at(100);

    return at1 + at2 + at3 + at4 + at5 + at6 + at7 + at8 + at9 + at10 + at11;

  • Code above can be simplified like this:

    • let text = "The light from the streetlamp was bright and eerie.";

    let indexs = [1, 2, 5, 4, 3, 1, 2, -10, 8, 2, -4];

    let sentence = "";


    for (let i = 0; i ≤ indexs.length; i ++) {

        sentence = text.at(indexs[i]);

    }


    return sentence;

    charAt()
  • The charAt() method returns the character at a specified index (position) in a string. The value cant be negative, and calling a value that is out of range will return an empty string.("")
    • Syntax:

    string.charAt(index)


    let text = "stay up, sport.";

    let indexs = [1, 11, 3, 11, 1, 2, 4, 0, 5, 6, 12, 2];

    let sentence = "";


    for (let i = 0; i ≤ indexs.length; i ++) {

        sentence = text.charAt(indexs[i]);

    }


    return sentence;

    charCodeAt()
  • The charCodeAt() method returns the Unicode UTF-16 of the character at a specified index (position) in a string. The method returns a number between 0 and 65535.
    • Syntax:

    string.charCodeAt(index)


    let text = "stay up, sport.";

    let indexs = [1, 11, 3, 11, 1, 2, 4, 0, 5, 6, 12, 2];

    let sentence = "";


    for (let i = 0; i ≤ indexs.length; i ++) {

        sentence = text.charCodeAt(indexs[i]) + " ";

    }


    return sentence;

    codePointAt()
  • The codePointAt() method returns the Unicode code point value at the specified index in a string. The method returns a non-negative integer that is the Unicode code point value.
    • Syntax:

    string.codePointAt(index)


    let text = "stay up, sport.";

    let indexs = [1, 11, 3, 11, 1, 2, 4, 0, 5, 6, 12, 2];

    let sentence = "";


    for (let i = 0; i ≤ indexs.length; i ++) {

        sentence = text.codePointAt(indexs[i]) + " ";

    }


    return sentence;

    concat()
  • The concat() method is used to join two or more strings. This method does not change the existing strings, but returns a new string containing the text of the joined strings.
    • Syntax:

    string.concat(string1, string2, ..., string2)


    let text1 = "Toyota";

    let text2 = "Supra";

    let result = text1.concat(" ", text2);

    constructor()
  • The constructor() method returns the string's constructor function.
    • Syntax:

    string.constructor


    let text = "Toyota Supra";

    let tcon = text.constructor;

    return tcon;

    endsWith()
  • The endsWith() method determines whether a string ends with the characters of a specified string, returning true or false as appropriate.
    • Syntax:

    string.endsWith(searchString, length)


    let text1 = ["Itachi Uchiha", "Sasuke Uchiha", "Naruto Uzumaki"];

    let text = "";


    for (let i = 0; i < text1.length; i++) {

        if (text1[i].endsWith("Uchiha")) text += text1[i] + " is from Uchiha clan" + "<br>";

        else text += text1[i] + " is not from Uchiha clan" + "<br>";

    }


    return text;

    fromCharCode()
  • The fromCharCode() method converts Unicode values into characters.
    • Syntax:

    String.fromCharCode(num1, num2, ...)


    let text = String.fromCharCode(116, 111, 121, 111, 116, 97, 32, 83, 117, 112, 114, 97);

    return text;

    includes()
  • The includes() method determines whether a string contains the characters of a specified string, returning true or false as appropriate.
    • Syntax:

    string.includes(searchString, position)

    Hidden Word: _ _ _ _ _

    indexOf()
  • The indexOf() method returns the position of the first occurrence of a specified value in a string. This method returns -1 if the value to search for never occurs.
  • It i simillar to String seach(), but the difference is:
  • The indexOf() method cannot search against regular expressions.
  • The search() cannot take a start position argument.
    • Syntax:

    string.indexOf(searchValue, fromIndex)


    let text = "Hello world, welcome to the hood.";

    let result = text.indexOf("welcome");

    return result;

    lastIndexOf()
  • The lastIndexOf() method returns the position of the last occurrence of a specified value in a string. This method returns -1 if the value to search for never occurs.
    • Syntax:

    string.lastIndexOf(searchValue, fromIndex)


    let text = "Hello planet earth, you are a great planet.";

    let result = text.lastIndexOf("planet");

    return result;

    length()
  • The length() method returns the length of a string (number of characters).
    • Syntax:

    string.length


    let password = ["vgN]fCGZ^Q_!nRPw", ":kJ*K=P", "AvdGGah>]6", "Ru8@:",
    "Rc(aW", "Y*xk33H$_", "_oqF^b|kc", "zY{y@f$'", "zCnct{HhU", "l(HOgMXhFQEhr", "?}&\\('|v"];

    let result = "";

    for (let i = 0; i < password.length; i++) {

        let stars = "";

        for (let j = 0; j < password[i].length; j++) {

            stars += "*";

        }

        if (password[i].length < 8) result += stars + " is too short" + "<br>";

        else result += stars + " is a good password" + "<br>";

    }

    return result;

    localeCompare()
  • The localeCompare() method returns a number indicating whether a reference string comes before, or after, or is the same as the given string in sort order.
    • Syntax:

    string.localeCompare(compareString)


    let text1 = "aaad";

    let text2 = "aaac";

    let result = text1.localeCompare(text2);

    let prt = "";


    if (result === -1) prt += "text1 is before text2";

    else if (result === 0) prt += "text1 equal to text2";

    else prt += "text1 is after text2";


    return prt;

    match()
  • The match() method retrieves the result of matching a string against a regular expression.
    • Syntax:

    string.match(regexp)


    let text1 = "No problem! Here's the information about the Mercedes CLR GTR:
    The Mercedes CLR GTR is a remarkable racing car celebrated for its outstanding performance and sleek design.
    Powered by a potent 6.0-liter V12 engine, it delivers over 600 horsepower. Acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h
    takes approximately 3.7 seconds, with a remarkable top speed surprising 320 km/h.🥇Incorporating
    adventure aerodynamic features and cutting-edge stability technologies, the CLR GTR ensures exceptional
    stability and control, particularly during high-speed maneuvers. 💨Originally priced at around $1.5 million,
    the Mercedes CLR GTR is considered one of the most exclusive and prestigious racing cars ever produced.
    💰Its limited production run of just five units adds to its rarity, making it highly sought after by racing
    enthusiasts and collectors worldwide. 🌎"    ;

    let text2 = "No problem!";

    let result = text1.match(text2);

    let prt = "";


    if (result != null) prt += "text1 is generated by AI";

    else prt += "text1 is written by hooman";

    return prt;

    padEnd()
  • The padEnd() method pads the current string with a given string (repeated, if needed) so that the resulting string reaches a given length.
    • Syntax:

    string.padEnd(targetLength, padString)


    let text1 = "69";

    let text2 = "420";

    let result = text1.padEnd(101, text2);

    return result;

    padStart()
  • The padStart() method pads the current string with another string (repeated, if needed) so that the resulting string reaches a given length.
    • Syntax:

    string.padStart(targetLength, padString)


    let text1 = "9";

    let text2 = "2024";

    let result = text1.padStart(2024, text2);

    return result;

    prototype()
  • The prototype() method allows you to add new properties and methods to the String object.
    • Syntax:

    string.prototype(name, function)


    function Person(firstName, lastName, age, eyeColor) {

        this.firstName = firstName;

        this.lastName = lastName;

        this.age = age;

        this.eyeColor = eyeColor;

    }

    Person.prototype.nationality = "Indonesian";

    const myFather = new Person('John', 'Doe', 50, 'blue');

    return "My father is " + myFather.nationality;

    repeat()
  • The repeat() method constructs and returns a new string which contains the specified number of copies of the string on which it was called, concatenated together.
    • Syntax:

    string.repeat(count)


    let text1 = "botol kecap marjan 5000 perak <br>";

    let result = text1.repeat(4);

    return result;

    replace()
  • The replace() method searches a string for a specified value, or a regular expression, and returns a new string where the specified values are replaced.
    • Syntax:

    string.replace(regexp, newvalue)


    let text1 = "Happy new year!. This new year will be a good one";

    let result = text1.replace("new year", "new day");

    return result;

    replaceAll()
  • The replaceAll() method returns a new string with all matches of a pattern replaced by a replacement.
    • Syntax:

    string.replaceAll(regexp, newvalue)


    let text1 = "Happy new year!. This new year will be a good one";

    let result = text1.replaceAll("new year", "new day");

    return result;

    search()
  • The search() method searches a string for a specified value, or regular expression, and returns the position of the first match.
    • Syntax:

    string.search(searchValue)


    let text1 = "lorem ipsum dolor sit amet consepcutor adispicing sit elit.";

    let result = text1.search("sit");

    return result;

    slice()
  • The slice() method extracts a section of a string and returns it as a new string, without modifying the original string.
    • Syntax:

    string.slice(start, end)


    let text1 = "The old heater, once a symbol of warmth, was now overshadowed by the cold,
    while the historian recounted tales of ancient symbols like 'Heil' in a lecture."    ;

    let result = text1.slice(136,140) + " " + text1.slice(8, 14);

    return result;

    split()
  • The split() method divides a string into an ordered list of substrings, puts these substrings into an array, and returns the array.
    • Syntax:

    string.split(separator, limit)


    let text1 = "The old heater, once a symbol of warmth, was now overshadowed by the cold,
    while the historian recounted tales of ancient symbols like 'Heil' in a lecture."    ;

    let words = text1.split(" ");

    return words;

    startsWith()
  • The startsWith() method determines whether a string begins with the characters of a specified string, returning true or false as appropriate.
    • Syntax:

    string.startsWith(searchString, position)


    let text1 = "The old heater, once a symbol of warmth, was now overshadowed by the cold,
    while the historian recounted tales of ancient symbols like 'Heil' in a lecture."    ;

    let result = text1.startsWith("Heil", 136);

    return result;

    substring()
  • The substring() method returns the part of the string between the start and end indexes, or to the end of the string.
    • Syntax:

    string.substring(start, end)


    let text1 = "The old heater, once a symbol of warmth, was now overshadowed by the cold,
    while the historian recounted tales of ancient symbols like 'Heil' in a lecture."    ;

    let result = text1.substring(20, 50);

    return result;

    substr()
  • The substr() method returns the characters in a string beginning at the specified location through the specified number of characters.
  • The usage of this method is discouraged. It's better to use substring() or slice() instead.
    • Syntax:

    string.substr(start, length)


    let text1 = "The old heater, once a symbol of warmth, was now overshadowed by the cold,
    while the historian recounted tales of ancient symbols like 'Heil' in a lecture."    ;

    let result = text1.substr(20, 50);

    return result;

    toLocaleLowerCase()
  • The toLocaleLowerCase() method returns the calling string value converted to lower case, according to any locale-specific case mappings.
    • Syntax:

    string.toLocaleLowerCase(locale)


    let text1 = "İstanbul'da güzel bir şehir.";

    let result = text1.toLocaleLowerCase('tr-TR');

    return result;

    toLocaleUpperCase()
  • The toLocaleUpperCase() method returns the calling string value converted to upper case, according to any locale-specific case mappings.
    • Syntax:

    string.toLocaleUpperCase(locale)


    let text1 = "The Greek word for 'sigma' is 'σ'.";

    let text2 = text1.substring(30, 32);

    let text3 = text2.toLocaleUpperCase('el-GR');

    let text4 = text1.replace(text2, text3);

    return text4;

    toLowerCase()
  • The toLowerCase() method returns the calling string value converted to lower case.
    • Syntax:

    string.toLowerCase()


    let text1 = "No problem! Here's the information about the Mercedes CLR GTR:";

    let result = text1.toLowerCase();

    return result;

    toString()
  • The toString() method returns a string representing the specified object.
  • Every object has a toString() method that is automatically called when the object is to be represented as a text value or when an object is referred to in a manner in which a string is expected.
  • It is also possible to call toString() on primitive values, although this is not common practice.
    • Syntax:

    object.toString()


    function car(brand, year) {

        this.brand = brand;

        this.year = year;

    }

    const supra = new car("Toyota Supra", 2020);

    let x = Object.values(supra).toString();

    let y = typeof(x);

    return x + "
    data type is: "     + y;

    toUpperCase()
  • The toUpperCase() method returns the calling string value converted to upper case.
    • Syntax:

    string.toUpperCase()


    let text1 = "The German term for 'sharp s' is 'ß'";

    let result = text1.toUpperCase();

    return result;

    trim()
  • The trim() method removes whitespace from both ends of a string.
  • Whitespace in this context is all the whitespace characters (space, tab, no-break space, etc.) and all the line terminator characters (LF, CR, etc.).
    • Syntax:

    string.trim()


    let text = " Toyota Supra ";

    let trimmedText = text.trim();

    return `Original Length: ${text.length}<br>

    Trimmed Length: ${trimmedText.length}<br>

    Original String: '${text}'<br>

    Trimmed String: '${trimmedText}'<br>

    Lengths are equal: ${text.length === trimmedText.length}`;

    trimEnd()
  • The trimEnd() method removes whitespace from the end of a string.
  • Whitespace in this context is all the whitespace characters (space, tab, no-break space, etc.) and all the line terminator characters (LF, CR, etc.).
    • Syntax:

    string.trimEnd()


    let text = " Toyota Supra ";

    let trimmedText = text.trimEnd();

    return `Original Length: ${text.length}<br>

    Trimmed Length: ${trimmedText.length}<br>

    Original String: '${text}'<br>

    Trimmed String: '${trimmedText}'<br>

    Lengths are equal: ${text.length === trimmedText.length}`;

    trimStart()
  • The trimStart() method removes whitespace from the beginning of a string.
  • Whitespace in this context is all the whitespace characters (space, tab, no-break space, etc.) and all the line terminator characters (LF, CR, etc.).
    • Syntax:

    string.trimStart()


    let text = " Toyota Supra ";

    let trimmedText = text.trimStart();

    return `Original Length: ${text.length}<br>

    Trimmed Length: ${trimmedText.length}<br>

    Original String: '${text}'<br>

    Trimmed String: '${trimmedText}'<br>

    Lengths are equal: ${text.length === trimmedText.length}`;

    valueOf()
  • The valueOf() method returns the primitive value of the specified object.
  • JavaScript calls the valueOf() method to convert an object to a primitive value when it is being used in a way that requires a primitive value.
  • For example, when an object is compared using the == operator, the JavaScript engine will call the valueOf() method to get the primitive value of the object.
    • Syntax:

    object.valueOf()


    let strObj = new String("Hello");

    return strObj.valueOf();

JavaScript Numbers

  • JavaScript has only one type of number. Numbers can be written with or without decimals.
    • Example:

    let x = 3.14;// A number with decimals

    let y = 3;// A number without decimals

  • Extra large or extra small numbers can be written with scientific (exponential) notation.
    • Example:

    let x = 123e5;// 12300000

    let y = 123e-5;// 0.00123

  • JavaScript Numbers are always 64-bit floating point
  • JavaScript does not have integers. JavaScript numbers are always stored as double precision floating point numbers, following the international IEEE 754 standard.
  • This format stores numbers in 64 bits, where the number (the fraction) is stored in bits 0 to 51, the exponent in bits 52 to 62, and the sign in bit 63.
  • Javascript numbers without period or exponentation are accurate up to 15 digits
    • Example:

    let x = 999999999999999;// x will be 999999999999999

    let y = 9999999999999999;// y will be 10000000000000000

  • The maximum number of decimals is 17.
    • Floating Precision
  • JavaScript numbers are stored in 64-bit floating point format, which means that the numbers are stored in binary format (base 2) instead of decimal format (base 10).
  • Due to this, some numbers cannot be represented accurately in the binary format, which can lead to unexpected results like this:

    • let result = 0.1 + 0.2;

    return result;

    Adding Numbers and Strings
  • JavaScript uses the + operator for both addition and concatenation.
  • Specifically for the addition (+), Numbers are added together, while strings are concatenated.

    • let result = 5 + 5;

    return result;


    let result = '5' + '5';

    return result;

  • Adding a number and a string will result in string concatenation:

    • let result = 5 + '2025';

    return result;

  • Some common mistake with addition is like this, if you add a string and a number, the result will be a string concatenation:

    • let result = 'The result is' + 4 + 20;

    return result;

  • While adding a number and then string will result in the number to be added first like this:

    • let result = 12 + 24 + '500';

    return result;

  • For other numeric operations, JavaScript will try to convert strings to numbers:

    • let result = '5' * '4';

    return result;

    NaN, Infinity, and Hexadecimal
  • NaN (Not a Number) is a JavaScript reserved word indicating that a number is not a legal number.
  • Trying to do arithmetic with a non-numeric string will result in NaN. However, if the string is numeric, the result will be the number:

    • let result = 100 / 'Apple'; // return NaN

    let result = 100 / '100'; // return 1

  • To find out if a value is a legal number in JavaScript, use the isNaN() function:

    • let result = isNaN(100 / 'Hello');

    return result;

  • NaN is a number: typeof NaN returns number. This mean, that it will be treated as a number in any operation.

  • Infinity is a number: typeof Infinity returns number. This mean, that it will be treated as a number in any operation.
  • Infinity (or -Infinity) is the value JavaScript will return if you calculate a number outside the largest possible number.

    • let myNumber = 2;


    while (myNumber != Infinity) {

        myNumber *= myNumber;

    }

    Note:

    be careful when doing an infinite loop though, because it might potentially just run indefinitely and freeze

  • Hexadecimal (base 16) numbers are written with a leading zero followed by an "x" (0x), followed by the hexadecimal number:

    • let result = 0x171717;

    return result;

  • Octal (base 8) numbers are written with a leading zero (0) followed by the octal number:

    • let result = 0171717;

    return result;

  • By default, JavaScript displays numbers as base 10 decimals. But you can use the toString() method to output numbers from base 2 to base 36.
  • Hexadecimal is base 16. Decimal is base 10. Octal is base 8. Binary is base 2.

    • let result = 255.toString(16); // will return 'ff'

    let result = 255.toString(8); // will return '377'

    let result = 255.toString(2); // will return '11111111'

    let result = 255.toString(10); // will return '255'

    Number as Objects
  • Normally, JavaScript numbers are primitive values created from literals:

    • let x = 123;

  • But numbers can also be defined as objects with the keyword new:

    • let x = new Number(123);

  • Do not create Number objects. It slows down execution speed, and prone to errors. Use numbers directly.
    • BigInt
  • BigInt is a new primitive type in JavaScript that can store whole numbers larger than 253 - 1, and lower than -(253 - 1).
  • BigInts are created by appending n to the end of an integer literal, or by calling the function BigInt().
  • Operators that can be used on a JavaScript number can also be used on a BigInt
  • However, it is to be noted that arithmetic operations between BigInt and Number are not allowed.

    • // BigInt literal

    let myBigInt = 2024202420242024202420242024202420242024202420242024n;

    let myType = typeof myBigInt;

    let myNumber = 2025;


    // arithmetic operations need to be the same data types

    let addition = myBigInt + BigInt(myNumber);

    return "typeof: " + myType "<br> addition: " + addition;

  • BigInt can also be written in hexadecimal, octal, or binary format:

    • let myBigInt = 0x1fffffffffffff;

    let myBigInt = 0o377777777777777777777n;

    let myBigInt = 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000011n;

    Number Methods
  • JavaScript has a number of useful methods to work with numbers.

    Number.constructor
  • Returns the function that created the Number object's prototype.
  • For JavaScript numbers, the constructor property returns:
  • function Number() { [native code] }

    • let x = 123;

    let y = x.constructor;

    return y;

    Number.EPSILON
  • Returns the smallest interval between two representable numbers. It can only be used as Number.EPSILON.
  • Using it as x.EPSILON where x is a number, will return undefined.
  • For JavaScript numbers, the EPSILON property returns:
  • 2.220446049250313e-16

    • return Number.EPSILON;

    Number.isFinite()
  • Returns true if the value is a finite number, otherwise false.
  • isFinite converts the value to a number before testing it, while Number.isFinite does not convert the value to a number.

    • let x = Number.isFinite('123');

    let y = isFinite('123');

    Number.isInteger()
  • Returns true if the value is an integer, otherwise false.

    • let x = 123;

    let y = -456;

    let z = '123';

    Number.isNaN()
  • Returns true if the value is NaN, otherwise false.
  • isNaN method returns true if the value is Not-a-Number
  • Number.isNaN only returns true if a number is Not-a-Number.

    • let x = Number.isNaN('Toyota Supra');

    let y = isNaN('Toyota Supra');

    Number.isSafeInteger()
  • Returns true if the value is a safe integer, otherwise false.
  • A safe integer is an integer that can be exactly represented as a IEEE-754 double precision number (all integers from -(253 - 1) to 253 - 1).

    • let x = 123;

    let y = -456;

    let z = 123456789012345678901234567890n;

    Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
  • Returns the largest safe integer in JavaScript (253 - 1) (9,007,199,254,740,991).
  • You can only use it as Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. Using x.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, where x is a variable, will return undefined.

    • let x = 9007199254740992;

    let y = 123456789;

    let z = -9007199254740991;

    Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER
  • Returns the smallest safe integer in JavaScript -(253 - 1) (-9,007,199,254,740,991).
  • You can only use it as Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER. Using x.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER, where x is a variable, will return undefined.

    • let x = 9007199254740992;

    let y = 123456789;

    let z = -9007199254740991;

    Number.MAX_VALUE
  • Returns the largest number possible in JavaScript.
  • Using it as x.MAX_VALUE where x is a number, will return undefined.

    • return Number.MAX_VALUE;

    Number.MIN_VALUE
  • Returns the smallest number possible in JavaScript.
  • Using it as x.MIN_VALUE where x is a number, will return undefined.

    • return Number.MIN_VALUE;

    Number.NaN
  • Returns NaN (Not-a-Number).
  • Using it as x.NaN where x is a number, will return undefined.

    • return Number.NaN;

    Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY
  • Returns negative infinity.
  • Using it as x.NEGATIVE_INFINITY where x is a number, will return undefined.

    • return Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;

    Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
  • Returns positive infinity.
  • Using it as x.POSITIVE_INFINITY where x is a number, will return undefined.

    • return Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;

    Number.parseFloat()
  • Parses a value as a string and returns the first floating point number found in the string.

    • Number.parseFloat("40.00");

    Number.parseFloat("    40    ");

    Number.parseFloat("40 years");

    Number.parseFloat("40H");

    Number.parseFloat("H40");

    Number.parseInt(string, radix)
  • Parses a value as a string and returns the first integer found in the string.
  • The radix parameter is optional. It specifies the base of the number. The default is 10.

    • Number.parseInt("10", 10);

    Number.parseInt("H010");

    Number.parseInt("10", 8);

    Number.parseInt("0x10");

    Number.parseInt("10", 16);

    Number.prototype
  • Allows you to add a new property or method to all numbers.
  • This new property or method will be accessible to all numbers.

    • Number.prototype.printHeilHeater = function() {

        let result = '';

        for(let i = 0; i < this; i++){

            result += "heil heater<br>";

        }

        return result;

    };


    let numb = 10;

    return numb.printHeilHeater();

    Warning!!

    It is not advised to change the prototype of an object that you do not control.

    You should not change the prototype of built-in JavaScript datatypes like:

    • String
    • Number
    • Array
    • Date
    • Function
    • Object
    Number.toExponential(digits)
  • Converts a number into an exponential notation.
  • The digits parameter is optional. It specifies the number of digits after the decimal point. Default is as many digits as necessary.

    • let num = 5.56789;

    let n = num.toExponential();

    return n;

    Number.toFixed(digits)
  • Converts a number into a string, keeping a specified number of decimals.
  • The digits parameter is optional. It specifies the number of digits after the decimal point. Default is 0.

    • let num = 5.56789;

    let n = num.toFixed(2);

    return n + "<br>typeof n is: " + typeof n;

    Number.toLocaleString(locales, options)
  • Converts a number into a string, using a local language format.

    • let num = 100000000;

    let text = num = num.toLocaleString("id-ID", {style:"currency", currency:"IDR"});

  • Below are the list of all parameter for toLocaleString() method:

    Number.toPrecision(digits)
  • Formats a number to a specified length.

    Number.valueOf()
  • Returns the primitive value of a number.
  • It is usually called automatically by JavaScript behind the scenes. The use case for calling it explicitly is when you need to make sure you are working with a primitive value.

    let num1 = new Number(10);

    let num2 = new Number("Toyota Supra");

JavaScript Arrays

  • JavaScript arrays are used to store multiple values in a single variable.
  • So imagine there is a list of items like below, storing in single variables would look like this:

    • let car1 = "Toyota Supra";

    let car2 = "Nissan Skyline";

    let car3 = "Mazda RX-7";

    let car4 = "Honda NSX";

    let car5 = "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution";

  • Now what if you want to loop through all the cars and find a specific one? And what if there is not 5 cars but like 300?
  • That's where arrays come in handy. Below is the syntax for a JavaScript Array

    • const array_name = [item1, item2, ...];

    Note!

    It is a common practice to use const when declaring an array. This is because you can still change the values inside the array, but you cannot reassign the array itself.

  • Below is array example for car above:

    • const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7", "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];

  • It is also possible to declare an array first and then provide the elements later:

    • const cars = [];

    cars[0] = "Toyota Supra";

    cars[1] = "Nissan Skyline";

    cars[2] = "Mazda RX-7";

    cars[3] = "Honda NSX";

    cars[4] = "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution";

  • The following example also creates an Array, and assigns values to it:

    • const cars = new Array("Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7", "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution");

  • However, it is advisable to just use the array literal method, and no need to use new Array() for simplicity, readability, and execution speed.
    • Accessing Array Elements
  • You refer to an array element by referring to the index number.
  • Array indexes start at 0. The first element in the array is [0], the second element is [1], and so on.

    • const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3", "Ford Mustang GT", "Chevrolet Camaro", "Porsche 911",
    "Audi R8", "Nissan GT-R", "Lamborghini Huracan", "Ferrari 488", "McLaren 720S", "Bugatti Chiron"];

    let result = "";


    function getOrdinal(n) {

        const suffixes = ["th", "st", "nd", "rd"];

        const value = n % 100;

        return n + (suffixes[(value - 20) % 10] || suffixes[value] || suffixes[0]);

    }


    for (let i = 0; i < cars.length; i++) {

        result += `${getOrdinal(i + 1)} car: ${cars[i]}
    `    ;

    }


    return result;

  • To change array element, it can be done like this:

    • const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3"];

    cars[1] = "Nissan Skyline GT-R";

  • The JavaScript method toString converts an array to a string of array values, separated by comma.
  • In this below example, i replace the comma into a <br>.

    • const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3"];

    let result = cars.toString().replaceAll(",", "<br>");

    return result;

  • Instead of using toString method, you can also access the full array by referring to the array name. The difference is that it will not be converted to a string.

    • const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3"];

    return cars + "<br> typeof cars: " + typeof cars;

  • As seen for the typeof array above, arrays are special type of objects. Array use numbers to access its "elements" while objects use names to access its "properties".

    • // This is how to access array

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3"];

    return cars[0];

    // This is how to access object

    const car = {"brand": "Toyota", "type": "Supra", "year": 2024};

    return car["brand"];

  • It is possible to have different type of variables in the same Array. It is possible to have objects, functions, or even another arrays inside an Array:

    • // Object

    const car = {

        "brand": "Toyota", "model": "Supra", "year": 2024, "features": ["Turbocharged engine", "Sport suspension", "Leather interior"]

    };


    // Function

    function calculateCarAge(year) {

        const currentYear = new Date().getFullYear();

        return currentYear - year;

    }


    // Inner Array

    const owners = ["Iqbal Dzakwan", "Fadoil Mun'im", "Gede Ardhi"];


    // Outer Array

    const carDetails = [car, calculateCarAge, owners];

  • To add a new element to an array, you can use the .push() method. This method adds a new element to the end of an array.

    • const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3"];

    cars.push("Nissan Skyline GT-R");

    Warning!!

    Adding elements with higher index than the current length of the array will create "empty slots".

    const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple"];

    fruits[6] = "Lemon"; // Creates undefined "holes" in fruits

    When to Use Arrays. When to Use Objects?
    • JavaScript does not support associative arrays.
    • You should use objects when you want the element names to be strings (text).
    • You should use arrays when you want the element names to be numbers.
  • The typeof operator will return object if used in array or an object. To solve this, there is 2 solution to check an array.

    • const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple"];

    Array.isArray(fruits) //first solution

    (fruits instanceof Array) //second solution

    JavaScript Array Methods and Properties
  • As seen above in the usage of .length, one of the real strength of arrays is the built-in properties and methods that can be used to manipulate the data.
  • Below are JavaScript array methods and properties:

    Array[]

    The [ ] constructor creates a new array object

    Syntax:

    [iterable]

    Example:

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7", "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];

    Parameters
    • iterable - An array-like or iterable object to convert to an array.
    Return Value
    • A new Array instance.
    Array()

    The new Array() constructor creates an Array object.

    Syntax:

    new Array(iterable)

    Example:

    const cars = new Array("Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7", "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution");

    Parameters
    • iterable - An array-like or iterable object to convert to an array.
    Return Value
    • A new Array instance.
    at()

    The at() method returns the element at the specified index in the array. It is the same as using bracket notation [].

    Syntax:

    array.at(index)

    Example:

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7", "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];


    cars.at(2);

    cars.at(-1);

    cars[2];

    cars[-1];

    Parameters
    • index - The index of the element to return. Can be negative, will start from the end of the array.
    Return Value
    • The element at the specified index in the array.
    concat()

    The concat() method is used to merge two or more arrays. This method does not change the existing arrays, but instead returns a new array.

    Syntax:

    array1.concat(array2, array3, ..., arrayX)

    Example:

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
    "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];

    const cars1 = ["Honda Civic", "Subaru BRZ", "BMW M3"];

    cars.concat(cars1);

    Parameters
    • array1, array2, ..., arrayX - Arrays to be merged into a new array.
    Return Value
    • A new Array instance.
    constructor

    The constructor property returns a reference to the array function that created the object.

    Syntax:

    array.constructor

    Example:

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
    "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];

    cars.constructor;

    Return Value
    • The function that created the object's prototype.
    copyWithin()

    The copyWithin() method shallow copies part of an array to another location in the same array and overwrites existing values it without modifying its length.

    Syntax:

    array.copyWithin(target, start, end)

    Example:

    const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango",
    "Kiwi", "Papaya", "Rambutan", "Durian"];

    fruits.copyWithin(2,0)

    fruits.copyWithin(2,0,3)

    Parameters
    • target - Required The index position to copy the elements to.
    • start - Optional The index position to start copying elements from.
    • end - Optional The index position to stop copying elements from.
    Return Value
    • The modified array.
    entries()

    The entries() method returns a new Array Iterator object that contains the key/value pairs for each index in the array.

    Syntax:

    array.entries()

    Example:

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Nissan Skyline", "Mazda RX-7",
    "Honda NSX", "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution"];

    let text = "";


    for (let i of cars.entries()) {

        text += i;

    }

    Return Value
    • An iterable object for the key/value pairs in the array.
    every()
    • The every() method executes a function for each array element.
    • If the function returns true for all elements, every() returns true. Otherwise, it returns false.
    • every() does not execute the function for empty elements.
    • every() does not change the original array.
    Syntax:

    array.every(function(currentValue, index, arr), thisValue)

    Example:

    const cars = ["Toyota Supra", "Toyota Camry", "Toyota Corolla",
    "Toyota RAV4", "Toyota Highlander", "Toyota Land Cruiser",
    "Honda Civic"];


    const allToyotas = cars.every(car => car.startsWith("Toyota"));

    Parameters
    • function() - Required A function to be run for each element in the array.
    • currentValue - Required The value of the current element.
    • index - Optional The array index of the current element.
    • arr - Optional The array object the current element belongs to.
    • thisValue - Optional. Default is undefined. A value to be passed to the function to be used as its this value.
    Return Value
    • true if the function returns a truthy value for every array element. Otherwise, false.
    fill()

    The fill() method fills the specified elements in an array with a static value.

    This method overwrites the original array.

    Syntax:

    array.fill(value, start, end)

    Example:

    const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango",
    "Kiwi", "Papaya", "Rambutan", "Durian"];


    fruits.fill("Lemon");

    fruits.fill("Lemon",2,4);

    Parameters
    • value - Required The value to fill the array with.
    • start - Optional The index position to start filling the array.
    • end - Optional The index position to stop filling the array.
    Return Value
    • The modified array.
    filter()

    The filter() method creates a new array with all elements that pass the test implemented by the provided function.

    If no elements pass the test, an empty array will be returned.

    filter() does not change the original array.

    Syntax:

    array.filter(function(currentValue, index, arr), thisValue)

    Example:

    const cars = [
        {car: "Toyota Supra", topSpeed: 155},
        {car: "Nissan Skyline", topSpeed: 180},
        {car: "Mazda RX-7", topSpeed: 155},
        {car: "Honda NSX", topSpeed: 170},
        {car: "Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution", topSpeed: 155},
        {car: "Subaru BRZ", topSpeed: 155}
    ];


    const result = cars.filter(topSpeed).map(car => car.car);

    function topSpeed(car) {

        return car.topSpeed >= 160;

    }

    Parameters
    • function() - Required A function to be run for each element in the array.
    • currentValue - Required The value of the current element.
    • index - Optional The array index of the current element.
    • arr - Optional The array object the current element belongs to.
    • thisValue - Optional. Default is undefined. A value to be passed to the function to be used as its this value.
    Return Value
    • An array with the elements that pass the test. If no elements pass the test, an empty array will be returned.
    find()

    The find() method returns the first element in an array that passes a test (provided as a function).

    The find() method executes a function for each array element.

    The find() method does not change the original array.
